Let’s dive into Chapter 2—The Science of Habit Formation: Why Habits Are So Hard to Change.
Now, you might be wondering, why do some habits stick with us, even when we really want to change them? Well, it all comes down to how our brains learn to crave the reward that follows a particular routine.
This craving takes over and becomes the driving force behind the habit loop, making certain behaviors feel almost irresistible.
Think back to a habit you’ve tried to form—maybe it’s going for a run after work. At first, you have to make a conscious decision every time; it takes effort and willpower. But as you keep repeating this, something interesting happens. Your brain starts to anticipate the reward—maybe that rush of endorphins or the simple satisfaction of sticking to your plan.
Over time, the decision-making part fades into the background. The moment the cue shows up, like finishing your workday, your brain craves that reward, and suddenly, the routine feels almost automatic.
And this isn’t just in your head—there’s real chemistry at play. When your brain expects a reward, it actually releases dopamine, the neurotransmitter that makes us feel pleasure and motivation. That burst of dopamine creates a sense of expectation, nudging you toward the routine, even if you’re busy or distracted.
Let’s make this real with a simple example. Imagine someone who bites their nails when they’re anxious. The cue? Anxiety. The routine? Nail-biting. The reward? A quick sense of relief. Over time, the brain connects those dots: cue, routine, reward. That craving for relief can get so strong, it overrides any conscious effort to stop—even if the person truly wants to quit.
Here’s something to pay close attention to: this is why willpower alone often falls short. The craving for that reward is so deeply wired, the behavior feels automatic.
But here’s the good news—you can actually use this same process to build new, healthier habits. If you understand how craving powers your habits, you can design new routines that give you what you need in a better way.
Let’s say someone’s trying to quit smoking. Maybe, what they’re really craving isn’t the cigarette itself, but a break from work or a moment to relax. If they swap that smoke break for a short walk or some deep breathing, keeping the same cue and reward, they can start to reshape the habit loop. The craving is still satisfied, but now with a healthier routine.
The science here is clear: habits aren’t destiny—they’re just patterns. And patterns can be understood, diagnosed, and changed. The secret is to pinpoint the craving that drives the loop, and then find new routines that match that need.
So, what practical steps can you take to change a habit? Here’s a quick rundown:
First, identify the cue. What triggers your behavior?
Next, pinpoint the routine—what action do you take after the cue?
Then, clarify the reward. What benefit are you actually getting?
Finally, experiment with new routines. Try different actions that still give you the same reward.
By looking at habits as a cycle powered by craving, you can take back control and make real, lasting changes. This way of thinking opens up the possibility for transformation—showing that even the toughest habits can be reshaped with the right approach.
